https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/ai-chatbot-hel.text: A mother and daughter who vanished during a trip to Europe reportedly asked an AI chatbot how to start a new life without being traced. Days later, investigators found them safe in Argentina. The information that reportedly helped police trace their journey included the history of their conversations with Google's Gemini chatbot.Mali Yahalomi and her daughter Liel were reported missing after disappearing in Vienna, Austria, in mid-August. Their disappearance prompted an international search as relatives and authorities tried to establish what had happened to them. Israeli media later reported that the two women had left voluntarily. According to reports, they had planned to start a new life abroad.The Questions They Asked AIBefore they disappeared, the women reportedly asked Gemini how to move to another country without being traced. Their reported questions included how to prevent a mobile phone from revealing their location and how to delete applications that could allow tracking.They also reportedly asked which South American countries did not have extradition agreements with Israel. At the time, neither woman was suspected of committing a crime in Israel. Other reported questions concerned obtaining a mobile phone without providing identification.Israeli media reported that the pair had considered changing their identities before starting a new life abroad. The reported Gemini conversations later became relevant to the investigation. According to The Times of Israel, investigators obtained access to the chatbot history, which helped them in their search for the missing women.A Journey Across ContinentsYahalomi and her daughter were last known to be in Vienna. Their disappearance was considered unusual and triggered a wide search involving Israeli authorities and police in other countries. Investigators later traced a journey that reportedly took the pair through several countries in Europe before they travelled to Argentina.Reports said the women bought a mobile phone in the Czech Republic and later travelled through Germany. They eventually continued to South America. Police located them on an intercity bus in Buenos Aires on August 16. Both were safe.They Said They Left VoluntarilyAfter they were found, the women spoke with Walter Kogan, an Israeli police representative in South America. They reportedly said they had left voluntarily and had not been threatened with violence. According to Channel 12, they said: We simply want to disconnect from the family, from the country.Police have not publicly established the full reason for their decision to leave Israel secretly. Some reports suggested that financial difficulties may have played a role. However, the precise reason for their departure remains unclear. The investigation did not find evidence that the women had been kidnapped or were victims of a violent crime.How Chatbot History Helped the SearchThe case has drawn attention because investigators reportedly used information from an AI chatbot while searching for the women.Google's privacy policy states that the company may disclose personal information when required to comply with applicable law, legal process or enforceable governmental requests. The company also says it reviews requests for user information and may challenge or seek to narrow requests it considers overly broad or legally invalid.This does not mean law enforcement can access every AI conversation without restrictions.The circumstances in which information can be disclosed depend on applicable law and legal processes. However, chatbot conversations can contain information that may become relevant to an investigation.In this case, investigators reportedly used the Gemini history to better understand the women's plans and movements.The information was considered alongside other evidence gathered during the international search.What the Case Shows About Digital RecordsThe Yahalomi investigation has highlighted the role that digital records can play in missing persons cases. AI chatbots allow users to ask questions about personal matters, travel and other subjects through conversational interfaces. Technology companies have different policies regarding the collection, retention, and management of user data.Google provides information about how data from its services is handled through its privacy policies and account settings. The company's policies also explain the circumstances in which it may respond to valid legal requests for user information.Users who want to understand how a particular AI service handles their information can review those policies directly. For Yahalomi and her daughter, the search began after they disappeared in Austria and ended when investigators found them safely in Argentina.The pair were not suspected of committing a crime. But investigators had to determine whether they were in danger or had left voluntarily. According to reports, the history of their conversations with an AI chatbot provided investigators with information that helped them locate the missing mother and daughter.

Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian Israel Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident Julian Borger and Quique Kierszenbaum in Petah Tikva Wed 21 Oct 2026 13.59 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 15.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians. Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah. It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers. Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet. “I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva. Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land. “Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said. She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene. “Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me. “I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye. “They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.” 1:57 American photojournalist recounts Israeli settler attack in the occupied West Bank – video Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety. “The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said. After the attack, Nathaniel wrote : “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.” He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge. Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.” Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog. “He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.” The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”. Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”. “That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.” The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh. On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody. Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”. “I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.” Explore more on these topics Israel West Bank Palestine Journalist safety Washington Post Benjamin Netanyahu US press and publishing news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Israeli military detain US and UK volunteers in West Bank including Democratic NY politician Brad Lander Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor US ambassador to Israel calls West Bank settler attack on American photojournalist ‘terror’ New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family UN adds 61 firms to settlements blacklist over alleged human rights violations against Palestinians Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk Will UK sanctions have any impact on Israel’s ‘settler terrorists’ in West Bank? What we know on day 1,709 Guardian staff and agencies Wed 28 Oct 2026 21.48 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 23.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A local ceasefire in southern Ukraine was holding for a second day , both sides said on Wednesday, as hopes grew that vital aid would be able to reach stranded residents. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in the Kherson region amid food and medical shortages and reports many people are now starving and eating weeds . The human rights ombudsmen of both Russia and Ukraine said on Wednesday the US-brokered truce – which came into effect early on Tuesday morning – was still holding . “30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky have passed without a single incident,” Ukraine’s Dmytro Lubinets said. “No incidents have been recorded in the 30 hours of the ceasefire in Oleshky,” Russia’s Yana Lantratova said in a similarly worded statement. The ceasefire would be guaranteed by “the physical presence of both ombudsmen: Ukrainian and Russian” on the ground, Lubinets’s office said. Route demining was “currently under way”, Lubinets said on social media, describing it as “crucial step toward ensuring the safe delivery of humanitarian aid and enabling civilians who wish to leave the city”. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that since the ceasefire came into force, there had been “no massive attacks” on the regional capital of Kherson , where about 280,000 people lived before Russia’s invasion. “We’re happy even when we have two, three days for these people. You know, some ceasefire is great, you can see them in the streets,” the Ukrainian president told reporters in The Hague. The truce would be a “huge success” if the evacuation of Oleshky’s citizens went ahead as planned, he said. The timing of the next round of three-way ⁠talks on a settlement of the Ukraine conflict is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, a Kremlin foreign policy aide has said , casting doubt on whether the talks will take place next month as initially proposed. Yuri Ushakov, quoted by Russian news ⁠agencies, said Moscow had not yet proposed a specific date for the talks. “It will ​also depend on the situation ‌on the battlefield and the ‌situation in general. You can see the situation now in the Middle East. It ‌just doesn’t allow us to hold it in the near future. That’s my assumption,” he told journalists on Wednesday. Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he hoped a meeting would take place in Abu Dhabi between 6 and 10 November. Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s “genius” and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder as Russia develops its own satellite communications for its military to use against Ukraine, reports Dan Sabbagh . The Russian president, speaking at a summit with African leaders in Moscow, was comparing the Earth-orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX with Russia’s gradual efforts to build its own Rassvet constellation. “Elon Musk is a genius, a true genius,” the Tass news agency quoted the Russian leader as saying. The Netherlands will supply Ukraine with €500m ($557m/£418m) ⁠in military support ⁠this ​winter , the Dutch prime minister said. The support ⁠would be used to supply drones and other material to ⁠strengthen Ukraine’s defence, Rob Jetten said ​after meeting Zelenskyy in The Hague. Earlier on ‌Wednesday, the Dutch government announced it would give Kyiv €1.2bn in non-military support in the next three years. Part of the money would be used for funds that supported ⁠Dutch companies willing to invest in the ​rebuilding ​of Ukraine. Russian authorities have issued permits for ⁠vessels carrying grain for export to leave the Sea of Azov for the first time since 10 July , ⁠when they closed maritime ⁠traffic ​in the area due to Ukrainian drone attacks, Reuters quoted seven industry sources as saying. They said permits to pass ⁠through the Kerch Strait, which links the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, would be issued for the period ⁠to 15 November.
